data.title: Gonorrhoea / urethral discharge — viva
data.summary: Sexually transmitted infections · 12 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Gonorrhoea / urethral discharge** (Sexually transmitted infections)_

**Q1. What is gonorrhoea? Organism?**
- STI caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae — Gram-negative intracellular kidney-shaped diplococcus; infects columnar/cuboidal epithelium (urethra, endocervix, rectum, pharynx, conjunctiva)
- Virulence: pili (attachment, antigenic variation), Opa proteins, porin, IgA1 protease, LOS (endotoxin)

**Q2. Clinical features in men and women.**
- Men: incubation 2–5 days; dysuria and profuse purulent urethral discharge; meatal oedema; ~10% asymptomatic
- Women: >50% asymptomatic; mucopurulent cervicitis, dysuria, vaginal discharge, intermenstrual bleeding
- Extragenital: rectal (receptive anal sex; proctitis), pharyngeal (mostly silent), ophthalmia

**Q3. Complications — local and metastatic (PYQ).**
- Men: epididymo-orchitis, prostatitis, periurethral abscess, Littre's gland and Tyson's gland infections, urethral stricture, infertility
- Women: Bartholin abscess, PID (salpingitis → infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain), Fitz-Hugh–Curtis perihepatitis
- Disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI, ~1%): arthritis–dermatitis syndrome — fever, tenosynovitis, migratory polyarthralgia, few acral haemorrhagic pustules on a red base; or septic monoarthritis; rarely endocarditis, meningitis (complement C5–C9 deficiency predisposes)
- Ophthalmia neonatorum (2–5 days after birth)

**Q4. Ophthalmia neonatorum (PYQ).**
- Conjunctivitis in first 4 weeks of life: gonococcal (2–5 days, hyperacute purulent, corneal perforation risk), chlamydial (5–14 days, milder), chemical (silver nitrate, first day)
- Gonococcal treatment: ceftriaxone 25–50 mg/kg IM single dose (max 125 mg) + saline eye irrigation; treat mother and partner
- Prophylaxis: erythromycin/tetracycline eye ointment or povidone-iodine at birth

**Q5. Approach to a case of urethral discharge (PYQ).**
- History: duration, incubation, nature of discharge, dysuria, sexual exposure and partners, previous episodes, antibiotic use
- Examine: milk the urethra, look at meatus, check epididymis, nodes, other STIs
- Gram stain of urethral smear: >2 (≥2–5) polymorphs per oil-immersion field = urethritis; Gram-negative intracellular diplococci = gonococcal (sensitivity >95% in symptomatic men)
- If no diplococci — non-gonococcal urethritis (Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma, Trichomonas, HSV, adenovirus)
- First-void urine NAAT for gonorrhoea and chlamydia (most sensitive); culture on Thayer–Martin/modified New York City medium for drug susceptibility
- Syndromic: NACO grey kit (azithromycin 1 g + cefixime 400 mg) to patient and partner

**Q6. Treatment of uncomplicated gonorrhoea.**
- Ceftriaxone single dose IM (500 mg current CDC/WHO; older guidelines 250 mg) plus treat chlamydia (doxycycline 100 mg BD × 7 days, or azithromycin 1 g) unless chlamydia excluded
- Alternative: cefixime 400–800 mg orally single dose; gentamicin 240 mg IM + azithromycin 2 g
- Abstain until 7 days after treatment and partner treated; test of cure for pharyngeal infection

**Q7. Discuss drug resistance in gonorrhoea (PYQ).**
- Sequentially lost penicillin (PPNG — plasmid β-lactamase), tetracycline (TRNG), fluoroquinolones (gyrA, parC), and now reduced susceptibility to cephalosporins (penA mosaic alleles) and azithromycin (23S rRNA, mtr efflux)
- Extensively drug-resistant strains reported (ceftriaxone-resistant FC428 clone); WHO priority pathogen
- Responses: higher ceftriaxone dose, culture and susceptibility surveillance (GASP), new oral drugs zoliflodacin and gepotidacin (recently approved in some countries — confirm current status)

**Q8. Discuss non-gonococcal urethritis (PYQ).**
- Commonest STI syndrome in men in many places; Chlamydia trachomatis serovars D–K (~30–50%), Mycoplasma genitalium (10–25%), Ureaplasma urealyticum, Trichomonas, HSV, adenovirus
- Incubation 1–3 weeks; mild mucoid discharge, dysuria; often asymptomatic
- Complications: epididymitis, reactive arthritis (urethritis, conjunctivitis, arthritis, keratoderma blennorrhagicum, circinate balanitis — HLA-B27), PID/infertility in women
- Treatment: doxycycline 100 mg BD × 7 days (preferred), azithromycin 1 g; M. genitalium — doxycycline then moxifloxacin (resistance-guided)

**Q9. What is Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome? (PYQ)**
- Perihepatitis complicating PID (Chlamydia > gonorrhoea) — right upper quadrant pain, pleuritic, 'violin-string' adhesions between liver capsule and abdominal wall on laparoscopy; LFT often normal

**Q10. How do you take a cervical sample?**
- Speculum examination, wipe ectocervix, insert swab 1–2 cm into endocervix, rotate 10–15 seconds; Gram stain less sensitive in women (50%) — prefer NAAT/culture

**Q11. Differentiate gonococcal and non-gonococcal urethritis clinically.**
- Gonococcal: shorter incubation (2–5 days), abrupt, profuse purulent yellow-green discharge, marked dysuria
- NGU: longer incubation (1–3 weeks), gradual, scanty mucoid/ watery discharge, mild dysuria, often early-morning 'glue' at meatus

**Q12. What is the Gram stain criterion for urethritis?**
- ≥2 polymorphonuclear leucocytes per oil-immersion field (×1000) in urethral smear (some use ≥5), or ≥10 PMN/hpf in first-void urine sediment, or positive leucocyte esterase

## Quick spotter facts
- Gram-negative intracellular diplococci in pus cells — gonorrhoea
- Acral haemorrhagic pustules + tenosynovitis — DGI
- Grey kit — urethral discharge

## Note
Ceftriaxone dose: newer guidelines use 500 mg (older 250 mg) — this is one of the open questions for the department.

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Gonorrhoea, non-gonococcal urethritis); NACO National Technical Guidelines on RTI/STI (syndromic management, colour-coded kits); WHO 2024 STI guidelines. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
